headline: Robot weapons, cautious shoppers and restless planets: deciding before we know
teaser: Should a machine ever decide to kill? Can exports hide weak spending at home? How far can we trust a model built on old data?

articles.title: Should Machines Decide Who Lives? The UN Debates "Killer Robots"
articles.dek: Governments meeting in Geneva are arguing over whether weapons that can choose and attack targets on their own need a new treaty. Can a principle survive when one country can block any deal?
paras: In a conference room in Geneva this week, diplomats began to tackle a question that once belonged to science fiction: should a machine ever be allowed to decide, on its own, to kill a human being? On Monday, November 16, talks on lethal autonomous weapons systems, often called "killer robots," opened at the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), a treaty that has limited cruel or indiscriminate weapons for more than 40 years. The central issue is simple to state but hard to settle: whether governments should finally begin negotiating binding rules for these weapons.

An autonomous weapon is different from the remote-controlled drones that have become common in recent wars. When a soldier flies a drone, a person still chooses the target and decides when to fire. An autonomous system, by contrast, can select and attack a target by itself once it has been activated, relying on sensors and software rather than a human operator. Because artificial intelligence and drone parts are becoming cheaper every year, many experts fear that such weapons could soon spread far beyond the world's largest militaries, a process known as proliferation.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres used a video message to urge delegates from more than 120 countries to start negotiating a legally binding instrument with "clear prohibitions and restrictions." The nature of warfare is changing, he argued, and new technologies raise humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges all at once. A few days earlier, the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, had put the moral case even more bluntly: "A machine must never have the power to decide whether a human being survives or dies."

Supporters of new rules make several arguments. The first concerns judgment: a machine does not understand the value of human life and cannot read a complicated situation the way a trained soldier can, for example by recognizing that a person is trying to surrender. The second concerns accountability. If an autonomous weapon kills civilians by mistake, it is unclear who should be held responsible — the commander, the programmer, or the company that built it. Last month, seven countries, including Austria, Brazil, Mexico and New Zealand, proposed a new legally binding agreement, and the campaign group Stop Killer Robots says about 130 countries now support new international rules.

Not every government agrees. According to the Associated Press, both the United States and Russia want to limit any restrictions on their ability to develop and deploy these systems, and Russia has described negotiations as "premature." Skeptics also make arguments of their own. Existing international humanitarian law, they point out, already applies to every weapon, so a new treaty may be unnecessary. Some go further, suggesting that well-designed machines, which do not panic or seek revenge, might one day identify targets more precisely than exhausted human soldiers and therefore reduce civilian deaths. Others note that defining "autonomy" is difficult, since many existing defense systems already react faster than any person could.

The structure of the CCW itself makes agreement harder. The treaty has 128 member states, and its decisions require consensus, which means that a single country can block any proposal. Supporters of a ban argue that this rule gives the most powerful militaries a veto over the rest of the world. Defenders of consensus reply that a treaty ignored by the countries that actually build these weapons would achieve little. History offers examples on both sides: when talks on landmines stalled in the 1990s, a group of countries moved outside the CCW and created the 1997 Ottawa Treaty, yet several major military powers never joined it.

There is, however, a hopeful precedent. In 1995, CCW members agreed to ban blinding laser weapons before they were ever widely used on the battlefield, showing that governments can act ahead of a new technology rather than after a disaster. More recently, in December 2023, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution confirming that autonomous weapons must respect the laws of war, with 152 countries in favor, four against and 11 abstaining.

Whatever happens in Geneva this week, the debate reaches beyond military strategy. It asks whether some decisions are so serious that they must always remain in human hands, even when a machine might be faster or, in some cases, more accurate. As the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, put it, states must act "to ensure the future of warfare is not handed over to machines." The difficult part is turning that principle into rules that every major power is willing to accept.

speak.p: Some people believe that decisions about life and death should always be made by humans, even if machines could make them faster or more accurately. Others believe we should use machines whenever they make fewer mistakes than people. Which view do you agree with, and why?
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (responsibility / judgment) + example → reason 2 (accuracy or speed) + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week, governments met in Geneva to discuss "killer robots", weapons that can select and attack targets without a human decision. The UN Secretary-General wants a legally binding treaty, but some major military powers say existing laws of war are enough. Should the world create a new treaty that bans or strictly limits these weapons? Why or why not? (Lena says: Yes. A machine cannot understand the value of a human life or tell when someone is trying to surrender. And if it kills the wrong person, nobody can be clearly blamed. We banned blinding lasers before they were used, so we should act now, before these weapons spread.) (Omar says: I'm not convinced a ban would work. The countries that build these weapons may simply refuse to sign, as some did with the landmine treaty. It might be more realistic to agree on rules that keep a human responsible for every attack, rather than an outright ban.)
steps: Decide your position: a ban, strict limits, or existing law.
Give one main reason, such as accountability or the risk of proliferation.
Respond to Lena or Omar: agree with one point and challenge another.
Finish with a clear one-sentence conclusion.

articles.title: Strong Exports, Cautious Shoppers: China's Economy Loses Momentum
articles.dek: October's figures show high-tech factories booming while households hold back. Should the government push people to spend, or is patience the wiser policy?
paras: China's economy lost more momentum in October, according to official figures released on Monday, November 16, by the National Bureau of Statistics. Retail sales, the main measure of how much households spend in shops and online, rose just 0.4 percent from a year earlier, half the 0.8 percent that economists polled by Reuters had expected and down from 1.1 percent in September. Industrial output grew 4.8 percent, also below forecasts of 5.3 percent and slower than September's 5.5 percent.

Investment looked even weaker. Fixed-asset investment, which counts spending on things such as factories, roads and buildings, fell 8.1 percent in the first ten months of the year compared with the same period in 2025, a worse result than analysts had predicted. Within that figure, property investment plunged 21.6 percent. There was one small piece of good news: the urban unemployment rate edged down to 5.1 percent from 5.2 percent. Economic growth for the third quarter had already slowed to 4.5 percent year on year.

Taken together, the numbers describe what some economists call a two-speed economy. On one side, factories making advanced products are booming. Officials said that high-end and intelligent manufacturing produced more than half of the growth in industrial output during the first ten months of the year, and exports linked to artificial intelligence, such as electronic components and equipment, remain strong. On the other side, traditional industries that depend on Chinese consumers and the construction sector are struggling. Strong exports, Reuters noted, are masking weakness in the domestic economy.

Why are households so cautious? The biggest reason is housing. For decades, buying an apartment was seen as the safest way for Chinese families to build wealth, so a large share of household savings is tied up in property. After a years-long slump in the housing market, many families feel poorer even if their incomes have not fallen, and people who feel poorer tend to spend less. A soft job market adds to the worry, especially for young graduates. As a result, many households prefer to save rather than buy cars, appliances or holidays.

This situation has produced a lively debate about what the government should do. One group of economists argues for stronger stimulus aimed directly at consumers. Lynn Song of the Dutch bank ING called the October figures "a worrying start" to the final quarter and said weak consumer confidence remained the main obstacle to recovery. In this view, measures such as larger pensions, better health insurance or cash support for families would give people the security they need to spend, which would in turn help the businesses that sell to them.

Others expect, and in some cases prefer, a more cautious approach. Analysts at the Australian bank ANZ said they did not expect new stimulus before the end of the year, and they forecast that annual growth would still stay above 4.5 percent. Economists at Macquarie predicted that policymakers would do "just enough" to meet their growth target, adjusting the size of any support according to how much exports slow. Supporters of restraint point out that earlier rounds of spending on infrastructure left many local governments with heavy debts, and that pushing money into the economy too quickly can be wasteful.

For their part, officials sounded confident. A statistics bureau spokesperson said exports would continue to support growth and that stronger policy support was coming. Beijing has recently introduced measures to channel cheaper credit into infrastructure and technology and to expand help for home buyers. These steps reflect a long-term goal: to move the economy away from construction and toward advanced industry. The open question is whether a strategy built on high-tech exports can succeed while consumers at home remain reluctant to spend.

The answer matters far beyond China. As the world's second-largest economy and its biggest exporter of manufactured goods, China affects prices, jobs and trade from Germany to Brazil. If Chinese households spend more, other countries can sell more to them; if China instead relies on exports, its trading partners may face more competition, and possibly more trade disputes. In that sense, the reluctance of shoppers in Chinese cities is not only a domestic issue but a global one.

speak.p: During an economic slowdown, some people think the government should give money directly to families to encourage spending. Others think it should invest in industries and infrastructure instead. Which approach do you prefer, and why?
speak.hint: Choose one approach → reason 1 + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: China's latest data show that high-tech exports are strong, but households are spending very little because the housing slump has made many families feel poorer. Some economists say the government should give money and security directly to families so they spend more. Others say it is better to keep investing in advanced industries and technology. If you were advising the government, which would you focus on, and why? (Wei says: I would focus on households. If people feel secure, for example with better pensions and health insurance, they will spend more, and shops and factories will benefit. An economy that depends only on exports is risky because other countries can buy less at any time.) (Sofia says: I think investing in advanced industries is wiser. Cash for families is spent once and then disappears, but new technology creates good jobs for many years. If young graduates find better jobs, they will start spending on their own.)
steps: Choose a focus: households, advanced industries, or a balance.
Give one main reason with an example.
Respond to Wei or Sofia: agree with one point and challenge another.
End with a clear one-sentence conclusion.

articles.title: Tilted and Restless: Solving the Puzzle of the Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields
articles.dek: A new computer model may explain why Uranus and Neptune have the strangest magnetic fields in the solar system. But how far can we trust a model built on two brief visits in the 1980s?

sources.name: ScienceDaily / University of Texas at Austin, Nov 15, 2026

paras: On Earth, a compass needle points roughly north because our planet's magnetic field is lined up fairly closely with the axis on which it spins, tilted by only about 11 degrees. When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft flew past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989, scientists expected to find something similar. Instead, they discovered two of the strangest magnetic fields in the solar system. Nearly four decades later, a new study published in the journal Communications Physics offers a possible explanation, along with a surprising prediction: these fields may change much faster than anyone thought.

To understand the puzzle, it helps to know how planets make magnetic fields. Deep inside Earth, a layer of molten iron flows and churns around the solid inner core. Because the moving metal conducts electricity, its motion generates electric currents, and those currents in turn produce a magnetic field. Scientists call this process a dynamo. Uranus and Neptune, known as ice giants, have no comparable iron ocean. Instead, much of their interior is thought to consist of water, ammonia and methane squeezed under enormous pressure and heat.

The fields that Voyager 2 measured looked nothing like Earth's. Uranus's magnetic field is tilted 59 degrees from its spin axis, and Neptune's is tilted 47 degrees. Even more oddly, neither field is centered on the middle of its planet; Uranus's appears shifted far toward the surface. One older idea linked Uranus's strange behavior to an ancient collision with an Earth-sized object, which may also explain why the planet spins on its side. That theory, however, cannot account for Neptune, which shows no sign of such a collision yet has a similarly odd field.

The new research, led by Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin with colleagues at UCLA, Imperial College London and Northumbria University, focuses on what happens to the planets' interiors with depth. Uranus is about 14.5 times as massive as Earth and Neptune about 17 times, so pressures inside them are crushing. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth," Yan explained. The team built computer simulations in which conductivity rises toward the center and found that these models could reproduce the unusual fields Voyager 2 recorded.

The simulations also produced a prediction. On Earth, the magnetic tilt drifts by only about a degree over 50 years. In the ice giant models, the behavior was far less steady: "In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades," Yan said, while in other periods it hardly changes. If this is correct, the fields measured by Voyager 2 in the 1980s may look quite different today, and an observer returning to Uranus might find its magnetic poles in new places.

Not everyone would treat the model as settled, and the authors themselves are careful. Simulations depend on assumptions, and nobody knows exactly what the inside of Uranus or Neptune is made of. The model was also tuned to match data gathered during two brief flybys, each offering only a snapshot of a planet's field at one moment. A model that reproduces old observations is plausible, critics might argue, but it is not the same as a model that has been confirmed by new ones.

Fortunately, there may be a way to test it without leaving Earth's neighborhood. Auroras — glowing lights produced when charged particles follow magnetic field lines into a planet's atmosphere — reveal where the magnetic poles lie. A team led by Tom Stallard of Northumbria University is analyzing James Webb Space Telescope images of auroras on both planets to check whether the poles have moved since the Voyager era. In the longer term, the researchers say, only a new spacecraft can fully verify the model. NASA has made a Uranus mission a priority for the early 2040s, and China's Tianwen-4 mission, due to launch toward Jupiter in 2029, is planned to release a small probe that will travel on to Uranus.

The puzzle matters beyond our own solar system. Planets roughly the size of Uranus and Neptune are among the most common types that astronomers have found orbiting other stars. Magnetic fields can shield a planet's atmosphere from streams of particles flowing out of its star, so understanding how ice giants generate theirs may help scientists judge which distant worlds could keep their atmospheres over billions of years. Two odd compass readings from the 1980s, in other words, may help explain planets we will never visit.
